scene: You meet your friend Marcus in the forum.
en: “Hello! How are you?” “I am well, thanks. And you?”
explain: _bene valeō_ = I am well (the _-ō_ is “I”). _grātiās_ = thanks. _Et tū?_ = and you? It hands the question back, as “and you?” does in English.
distractors: “And you” as the person asked is the nominative: _tū_, not _tē_.

en: “Where are you walking to?” “I am walking to the baths.”
explain: _quō?_ asks “where to?”, so the answer uses _ad_ + accusative: _ad thermās_. _ambulō_ is “I walk”.
distractors: _ad_ takes the accusative: _thermās_, not the nominative _thermae_.
_ex thermīs_ means “out of the baths”. The question asks where you are going to: _ad thermās_.

en: “Why are you walking to the baths?” “I want to wash.”
explain: _cūr?_ asks “why?”. “I want to wash” is _lavāre volō_: _volō_ + the infinitive (_lavāre_, to wash).
distractors: After _volō_ use the infinitive: _lavāre_ (to wash), not _lavō_ (I wash).
_nōlō_ means “I do not want”. You want to wash: _volō_.

explain: _grātiās tibi agō_ is “I give thanks to you”, the usual way to say thank you. _tibi_ is “to you” (dative).

scene: A new neighbor speaks to you at the garden gate.
q: Salvē, hospes! Quid tibi nōmen est?
en: “Hello, guest! What is your name?” “Hello! My name is Paul.”
explain: _mihi nōmen est Paulus_ is “my name is Paul” (literally “to me the name is Paul”). The name stays nominative.
distractors: “My name is” needs _est_ (it is). _es_ means “you are”.
“My name is…” uses the dative: _mihi nōmen est_.

en: “Hello, Paul! Where do you come from?” “I come from America.”
modernNote: America was unknown to the Romans, so this is a modern name with Latin endings.
explain: _unde?_ asks “from where?”. A country needs _ex_ (“out of”) plus the ablative: _ex Americā_. _veniō_ is “I come”.
distractors: _in Americā_ means “in America”. “From America” is _ex Americā_.

en: “Where do you live?” “I live in Italy.”
explain: _ubi?_ asks “where?”. A country needs _in_ + ablative: _in Italiā_. (A town like _Rōmae_ needs no _in_.) _habitō_ is “I live”.
distractors: _in_ + accusative means “into”. For “in Italy” use the ablative: _in Italiā_.
_ex Italiā_ means “out of Italy”. “In Italy” is _in Italiā_.

en: “Do you have friends in Italy?” “Yes, I have friends.”
explain: _-ne_ makes a yes/no question. _amīcōs_ is accusative plural: the friends are what you have.
distractors: What you have is the object: accusative plural _amīcōs_, not nominative _amīcī_.
_minimē_ means “no”. The answer here is yes: _etiam_.

scene: A new friend asks about your family.
en: “Do you have a sister?” “Yes, I have a sister. She is Julia.”
explain: _sorōrem_ is accusative singular, the thing you have. _Iūlia est_ = she is Julia (_est_ = he/she/it is).
distractors: What you have is the object: accusative _sorōrem_, not nominative _soror_.

en: “Where does Julia live?” “She lives in Rome.”
explain: _Rōmae_ is the locative, “at Rome”, with no _in_. _habitat_ is “she lives”: the ending _-t_ is “he/she”.
distractors: _habitō_ is “I live”. The question is about Julia: _habitat_.
_habitant_ is “they live”. Julia is one person: _habitat_.
